claim: Angpt4 is expressed in a specific sub-population of astrocytes at the site where venous morphogenesis occurs in mouse retina.
source: By using genetic reporter, fate mapping, and in situ hybridization, we found Angpt4 expression in a specific sub-population of astrocytes at the site where venous morphogenesis occurs
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from genetic reporter mice (Angpt4LacZ and Angpt4Cre; Rosa26mT/mG), fate mapping, and in situ hybridization experiments shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Lower oxygen tension enhances Angpt4 expression in retinal astrocytes.
source: lower oxygen tension, which distinguishes peripheral and venous locations, enhances Angpt4 expression
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased Angpt4+ astrocytes in low oxygen conditions (Figure 2E-H) and in OIR model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and by conditional deletion of Egln1 (Figure 2H).

claim: Deletion of Angpt4 results in defective venous development in mouse retina.
source: deletion of Angpt4 resulted in defective venous development causing impaired venous drainage and defects in neuronal cells
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Angpt4-/- mice showing weak αSMA staining around veins (Figure 4A-B), reduced vein diameter (Figure 4J-K), and ultrastructural abnormalities (Figure 5).

claim: Angpt4 deficiency causes impaired venous drainage in the retina.
source: deletion of Angpt4 resulted in defective venous development causing impaired venous drainage and defects in neuronal cells
evidence: The claim is supported by functional data from fluorescein angiography showing decreased venous filling (Figure 7A-E) and fluorosphere retention experiments showing slower draining (Figure 7F-H).

claim: Angpt4 deficiency leads to defects in neuronal cells in the inner nuclear layer of the retina.
source: deletion of Angpt4 resulted in defective venous development causing impaired venous drainage and defects in neuronal cells
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data showing increased INL thickness (Figure 6A-B) and ultrastructural evidence of cell swelling in adult Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 6D).

claim: Angpt4 is the first growth factor identified for venous-specific development.
source: Our study identifies Angpt4 as the first growth factor for venous-specific development and its importance in venous remodeling, retinal fluid clearance and neuronal function.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that Angpt4 deficiency specifically affects veins but not arteries or capillaries (Figure 4), which differs from other known growth factors. This represents a novel finding in the field.

claim: Angpt4 expressing cells are strongly enriched in the peripheral retina by postnatal day 9.
source: Angpt4 expressing cells were strongly enriched by P9 in Angpt4LacZ mice (Figure 1A), at the time when peripheral venous maturation occurs (Crist et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by X-gal staining data from Angpt4LacZ mice at P9 (Figure 1A) and GFP expression in Angpt4Cre; Rosa26mT/mG mice (Figure 1C-G).

claim: At P20, when maturation of retinal vasculature is nearly completed, Angpt4 expressing cells are decreased in number.
source: At P20 (Figure 1B), when maturation of retinal vasculature is nearly completed, Angpt4 expressing cells were decreased in number and thereafter only few were observed close to the veins and perivenous capillaries.
evidence: The claim is supported by X-gal staining data from Angpt4LacZ mice at P20 showing fewer Angpt4 expressing cells compared to P9 (Figure 1B).

claim: During venous development, Angpt4 expressing cells are preferentially located in the peripheral segments while central retina is virtually negative.
source: During venous development, in both independent mouse lines, Angpt4 expressing cells were not randomly positioned but preferentially located in the peripheral segments while central retina was virtually negative (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data from both Angpt4LacZ and Angpt4Cre; Rosa26mT/mG mice showing enrichment of Angpt4+ cells in peripheral retina (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Angpt4 expressing cells are astrocytes based on their morphology, position in the superficial retinal layer, and GFAP expression.
source: Based on their morphology, position in the superficial retinal layer, and specific cell marker gene (GFAP) expression, we identified Angpt4 expressing cells as astrocytes (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing colocalization of GFP+ cells with GFAP staining (Figure 2D) and their location in the superficial retinal layer (Figure 2C).

claim: Angpt4+ astrocytes are less numerous close to arteries where oxygen tension is higher than in veins.
source: In addition, Angpt4+ astrocytes were less numerous close to arteries (Figure 2A–B) where oxygen tension is higher than in veins.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative imaging data showing fewer GFP+ cells near arteries compared to veins in adult retina (Figure 2A-B).

claim: Exposure to low oxygen atmosphere increases the number of Angpt4+ astrocytes in mouse retina.
source: To confirm that low oxygen level positively regulates Angpt4 expression, Angpt4Cre/+; Rosa26mT/mG mice were exposed to low oxygen atmosphere (Figure 2E–G) and retinal ischemia (OIR model, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E) that both increased the number of Angpt4+ astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased GFP+ cells in mice exposed to 12% O2 compared to normoxia (Figure 2E-G).

claim: Retinal ischemia in the OIR model increases the number of Angpt4+ astrocytes.
source: To confirm that low oxygen level positively regulates Angpt4 expression, Angpt4Cre/+; Rosa26mT/mG mice were exposed to low oxygen atmosphere (Figure 2E–G) and retinal ischemia (OIR model, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E) that both increased the number of Angpt4+ astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased GFP+ cells in the OIR model at P17 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B).

claim: Angpt4 expression is positively regulated by HIF prolyl-hydroxylase 2 (Egln1)-dependent hypoxia pathway.
source: By using conditional genetic depletion, we further confirmed that Angpt4 expression is positively regulated by HIF prolyl-hydroxylase 2 (Egln1) -dependent hypoxia pathway (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data showing increased Angpt4 mRNA in Angpt4Cre; Egln1loxP/loxP mice compared to controls (Figure 2H).

claim: In hyperoxia, Angpt1 mRNA expression is decreased while Angpt2 and Angpt4 mRNA levels increase in the retina.
source: In hyperoxia, which in short-term promotes astrocyte differentiation (Duan et al., 2017), in long-term causes retinal degeneration (Yamada et al., 1999) and paradoxically can cause hypoxia by blocking vascular development in the retina (West et al., 2005), Angpt1 mRNA expression was decreased while Angpt2 and Angpt4 mRNA levels increased.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data from eyes exposed to 75% O2 compared to normoxia (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).

claim: At P3, Angpt4 mRNA expression precedes the growing vascular front in the retina.
source: At P3, Angpt4 in situ signal was found consistently and it preceded the growing vascular front (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing Angpt4 expression ahead of the vascular front at P3 (Figure 3A).

claim: At P12, Angpt4 mRNA is enriched in astrocytes in the peripheral retina.
source: At P12, Angpt4 mRNA was enriched in the astrocytes in the peripheral retina (Figure 3B), while no specific staining was detected in Angpt4-/- retina (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing Angpt4 mRNA signal colocalizing with GFAP+ astrocytes in peripheral retina at P12 (Figure 3B).

claim: Angpt1 mRNA is not detectable in the peripheral retina at P12 by whole mount in situ hybridization.
source: In the peripheral retina, Angpt1 mRNA was not detectable at P12 (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing no Angpt1 signal in peripheral retina at P12 (Figure 3C), although the probe was validated in P4 retina and P2 atriums (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G-J).

claim: Angpt2 mRNA is expressed in neuron cells in the intermediate layers of retina at P12.
source: while Angpt2 mRNA was found to be expressed in neuron cells in the intermediate layers of retina (Figure 3D) as reported earlier (Hackett et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing Angpt2 expression in intermediate retinal layers (Figure 3D) and is consistent with previous reports.

claim: Tie2 mRNA is localized in endothelial cells in veins, arteries and capillaries at P12.
source: Tie2 mRNA was localized in ECs in veins, arteries and capillaries (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data showing Tie2 expression in endothelium of all vessel types (Figure 3E).

claim: Angpt4Cre/Cre mice lack Angpt4 mRNA expression.
source: RT-qPCR confirmed the lack of Angpt4 mRNA in Angpt4Cre/Cre mice (hereafter Angpt4-/-) and no compensatory change in Angpt1 or Angpt2 was detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data showing no Angpt4 mRNA in Angpt4Cre/Cre eyes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Angpt4 deficiency does not cause compensatory changes in Angpt1 or Angpt2 mRNA expression.
source: RT-qPCR confirmed the lack of Angpt4 mRNA in Angpt4Cre/Cre mice (hereafter Angpt4-/-) and no compensatory change in Angpt1 or Angpt2 was detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data showing no significant changes in Angpt1 or Angpt2 mRNA levels in Angpt4-/- eyes at P12 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Angpt4-/- mice show weak alpha smooth muscle actin (αSMA) immunofluorescence in smooth muscle cells around forming veins in the peripheral retina at P12.
source: As a first implication of a vascular phenotype, we observed weak alpha smooth muscle actin (αSMA) immunofluorescence in Angpt4-/- SMCs around the forming veins in the peripheral part of the retina at P12 (Figure 4A–B), correlating well with the spatiotemporal Angpt4 expression pattern.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data comparing αSMA staining in WT and Angpt4-/- retinas at P12 (Figure 4A-B).

claim: The low αSMA expression defect around veins in Angpt4-/- mice persists into adulthood.
source: The low αSMA expression defect around veins persisted into adulthood (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data from 9-month-old mice showing reduced αSMA staining around peripheral veins in Angpt4-/- retinas (Figure 4C-G).

claim: The diameter of peripheral veins in Angpt4-/- mice does not increase during development.
source: Furthermore, the diameter of peripheral veins did not increase during development (Figure 4J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements showing reduced peripheral vein diameter in Angpt4-/- mice at both P12 and adult stages (Figure 4J).

claim: Defective vascular morphogenesis in Angpt4-/- mice is observed in veins preferentially in the peripheral retina but not in central retina close to the optic nerve head.
source: In both P12 and adult mice, the defective vascular morphogenesis was observed in the veins and preferentially in those locating at retina's periphery but not in central retina close to the optic nerve head (Figure 4G–H,J–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data showing reduced αSMA intensity and vein diameter in peripheral but not central veins (Figure 4G-H, J-K).

claim: Arteries, peripheral arterioles and capillaries remain unaffected in Angpt4-/- mice.
source: In addition, arteries, peripheral arterioles and capillaries remained unaffected (Figure 4C–F,I)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing normal αSMA staining around arteries (Figure 4C-F, I) in Angpt4-/- mice.

claim: No consistent alterations are observed in the vasculature of the intermediate or deep vascular plexuses in Angpt4-/- mice postnatally or in adults.
source: and no consistent alterations were observed in the vasculature of the intermediate or deep vascular plexuses postnatally or in adults (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological and imaging data showing normal vessel density in deeper plexuses (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-I).

claim: Smooth muscle cells in peripheral veins of Angpt4-/- mice lack cellular and molecular characteristics of matured SMCs based on ultrastructural analysis.
source: At later time points, however, ultrastructural analysis revealed lack of cellular and molecular characteristics of matured SMCs in Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 5B–F,M–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data showing reduced myofilaments and fibrillar collagen in Angpt4-/- venous SMCs (Figure 5B-F, M-N).

claim: SM22, a marker of adult smooth muscle cells, is greatly reduced around Angpt4-/- veins.
source: To confirm defective maturation, whole mount retinas were stained for SM22, a marker of adult SMCs (Li et al., 1996), which was greatly reduced around Angpt4-/- veins (Figure 5G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing reduced SM22 staining around veins in 2-month-old Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 5G-J).

claim: Angpt4 is required for smooth muscle cell maturation but not for SMC recruitment, proliferation or survival.
source: Collectively, these experiments indicated that Angpt4 is required for SMC maturation, but not for SMC recruitment, proliferation or survival and that Angpt4 does not directly signal to SMCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by ultrastructural data showing defective SMC maturation (Figure 5), negative results from SMC proliferation, migration, and apoptosis assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C), and TIE2 expression data (Figure 5K).

claim: TIE2 receptor is expressed predominantly in human endothelial cells, but also in smooth muscle cells isolated from adult human veins or arteries.
source: In vitro, angiopoietin receptor TIE2 was expressed predominantly in human ECs, but also in SMCs isolated from adult human veins or arteries (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data showing TIE2 expression in HUVECs, arterial SMCs, and venous SMCs (Figure 5K).

claim: Excess ANGPT4 does not increase smooth muscle cell survival in Caspase 3/7 ELISA.
source: Excess of ANGPT4, however, did not increase SMC survival in Caspase 3/7 ELISA and did not promote SMC migration in scratch assay or their proliferation in BrdU ELISA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Caspase 3/7 assays showing no effect of ANGPT4 on SMC apoptosis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Excess ANGPT4 does not promote smooth muscle cell migration in scratch assay.
source: Excess of ANGPT4, however, did not increase SMC survival in Caspase 3/7 ELISA and did not promote SMC migration in scratch assay or their proliferation in BrdU ELISA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from scratch assays showing no effect of ANGPT4 on SMC migration (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Excess ANGPT4 does not promote smooth muscle cell proliferation in BrdU ELISA.
source: Excess of ANGPT4, however, did not increase SMC survival in Caspase 3/7 ELISA and did not promote SMC migration in scratch assay or their proliferation in BrdU ELISA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from BrdU assays showing no effect of ANGPT4 on SMC proliferation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: qPCR from Angpt4-/- retinas shows a decrease in Tie2 expression.
source: qPCR from retinas did not reveal statistically significant changes in factors previously implicated in venous development, except a decrease in Tie2 (Figure 5L).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data showing reduced Tie2 mRNA in Angpt4-/- retinas at P12 (Figure 5L).

claim: The thickness of the inner nuclear layer is increased in adult Angpt4-/- retinas.
source: In light microscopy, the thickness of the INL was increased in adult Angpt4-/- retinas (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological measurements from toluidine blue and Masson's trichrome stained sections showing increased INL thickness in Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 6A-B).

claim: TEM reveals enlarged, cell-organelle-free cytoplasm in neuronal cell somas in adult Angpt4-/- inner nuclear layer.
source: TEM revealed enlarged, cell-organelle-free cytoplasm in neuronal cell somas in adult INL (Figure 6D), a phenotype that closely resembled ultrastructural changes of swollen cells (Łotowska et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data showing increased cell soma area with reduced organelle density in adult Angpt4-/- INL (Figure 6D).

claim: The normal architecture of Müller cells is lost around swollen cell bodies in adult Angpt4-/- retinas.
source: In addition, the normal architecture of Müller cells that have a specialized function in retinal ﬂuid management expressing specific channels for water efflux (Spaide, 2016) was lost around the swollen cell bodies.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data showing displaced Müller cell processes around swollen cells in adult Angpt4-/- retinas (Figure 6D).

claim: Neuronal cell changes in Angpt4-/- mice are not seen at P13 but are present in adult mice.
source: These changes were not seen in P13 mice (Figure 6C). In adult mice, however, we found no alterations in the expression of AQP4 water (1.0 ± 0.2 vs.1.9 ± 1.5) or Kir4.1 potassium channels (1.0 ± 0.1 vs. 1.1 ± 0.3) (WT vs. Angpt4-/-, mean ±SD, WT value set to 1, n = 3 in both genotypes, p=NS in t-test). Comparison of P13 and adult mice revealed that changes in neuronal cells occurred after defective venous development (Figure 6C–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data showing normal cell soma area at P13 but increased area in adult Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 6C-D).

claim: Changes in neuronal cells in Angpt4-/- mice are not found in other retinal layers than the inner nuclear layer.
source: and were not found in other retinal layers than in INL (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data showing normal ultrastructure in outer and superficial retinal layers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D).

claim: There is no evidence of cystoid edema or inflammation in Angpt4-/- retinas.
source: We observed no evidence of cystoid edema or inflammation (lack of fluid-filled cysts and cellular infiltration in histology in Figure 6A–B and in ultrastructure in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D, and no increase in general inflammation markers in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological and ultrastructural data showing no fluid-filled cysts or cellular infiltration (Figure 6A-B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D) and qPCR data showing no increase in inflammation markers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B).

claim: Venous filling in relation to arteries is decreased in the early phase of fluorescein angiography in Angpt4-/- mice.
source: In the early phase, venous filling in relation to arteries was decreased in Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 7A,C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescein angiography data showing reduced venous fluorescence intensity relative to arteries in Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 7A, C, E).

claim: No vascular leakage is observed in the peak phase of fluorescence in fluorescein angiography of Angpt4-/- mice.
source: No leakage was observed in the peak phase of fluorescence (Figure 7B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescein angiography images showing no evidence of dye leakage at peak fluorescence (Figure 7B, D).

claim: Retention of fluorospheres is evident in the peripheral annular vein bifurcation sites in Angpt4-/- mice, suggesting slower draining time than in controls.
source: In Angpt4-/- mice, retention of fluorospheres was evident in the peripheral annular vein bifurcation sites, suggesting slower draining time than in controls (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorosphere injection experiments showing increased sphere retention in peripheral veins of Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 7F-H).

claim: In aged (eight month) Angpt4-/- mice, flash electroretinography demonstrates a decrease in b-wave amplitude.
source: In aged (eight mo) Angpt4-/- mice, fERG demonstrated a decrease in b-wave amplitude that measures the activity of the bipolar, Müller and amacrine cells (Figure 7I).
evidence: The claim is supported by electroretinography data showing reduced b-wave amplitudes at multiple flash intensities in 8-month-old Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 7I).

claim: The a-wave amplitude in flash electroretinography is not affected in aged Angpt4-/- mice.
source: In contrast, a-wave amplitude, generated by photoreceptors, was not affected (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by electroretinography data showing no significant difference in a-wave amplitudes (Figure 7—source data 1).

claim: There is no evidence for vascular leakage in Angpt4-/- mice based on fluorescein angiography.
source: We found no evidence for vascular leakage in fluorescein angiography (Figure 7D) or hypoxia (negative pimonidazole staining and mRNA markers in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescein angiography showing no leakage (Figure 7D).

claim: There is no evidence for hypoxia in Angpt4-/- retinas based on pimonidazole staining and mRNA markers.
source: We found no evidence for vascular leakage in fluorescein angiography (Figure 7D) or hypoxia (negative pimonidazole staining and mRNA markers in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by negative pimonidazole immunostaining and no increase in Vegfa or Angpt2 mRNA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-D).

claim: Angpt4 and ANGPT4 induce growth of luminal structures in HUVEC spheroids in a TIE2-dependent manner.
source: Using inhibitors against plasmin/serine proteases (aprotinin), PI3K (BYL719 and LY294002) and shRNA constructs directed against TIE2 (Figure 8A–D), we found that similarly to ANGPT1, Angpt4 and ANGPT4 induced growth of luminal structures TIE2, PI3K and serine protease dependently.
evidence: The claim is supported by fibrin gel spheroid assay data showing reduced lumen formation when TIE2 is knocked down (Figure 8C-D).

claim: Angpt4 and ANGPT4 induce growth of luminal structures in HUVEC spheroids in a PI3K-dependent manner.
source: Using inhibitors against plasmin/serine proteases (aprotinin), PI3K (BYL719 and LY294002) and shRNA constructs directed against TIE2 (Figure 8A–D), we found that similarly to ANGPT1, Angpt4 and ANGPT4 induced growth of luminal structures TIE2, PI3K and serine protease dependently.
evidence: The claim is supported by fibrin gel spheroid assay data showing reduced lumen formation in the presence of PI3K inhibitors BYL719 and LY294002 (Figure 8A-B).

claim: Angpt4 and ANGPT4 induce growth of luminal structures in HUVEC spheroids in a serine protease-dependent manner.
source: Using inhibitors against plasmin/serine proteases (aprotinin), PI3K (BYL719 and LY294002) and shRNA constructs directed against TIE2 (Figure 8A–D), we found that similarly to ANGPT1, Angpt4 and ANGPT4 induced growth of luminal structures TIE2, PI3K and serine protease dependently.
evidence: The claim is supported by fibrin gel spheroid assay data showing reduced lumen formation in the presence of aprotinin (Figure 8A-B).

claim: ANGPT4-induced lumen enlargement is not enhanced by smooth muscle cells in co-culture spheroid model.
source: In a co-culture spheroid model, ANGPT4-induced lumen enlargement was not enhanced by SMCs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) and SMC spheroids alone did not respond to ANGPT4 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-culture spheroid data showing no additional lumen formation when SMCs are present (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Smooth muscle cell spheroids alone do not respond to ANGPT4.
source: In a co-culture spheroid model, ANGPT4-induced lumen enlargement was not enhanced by SMCs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A) and SMC spheroids alone did not respond to ANGPT4 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by spheroid assay data showing no lumen formation in SMC-only spheroids treated with ANGPT4 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The vascular phenotype in Angpt4-/- retinas is clearly different from that observed in mice lacking Angpt1 or Angpt2.
source: The observed phenotype in Angpt4-/- retinas was clearly different from that observed in mice lacking Angpt1 (Lee et al., 2013) or Angpt2 (Gale et al., 2002; Hackett et al., 2002) that both result in reduced growth of primary capillary plexus and not in vein-specific phenotype.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the venous-specific phenotype in Angpt4-/- mice with published phenotypes of Angpt1-/- and Angpt2-/- mice showing capillary defects.

claim: In the OIR model, Angpt1 and Angpt2 deletions reduce neovascular tuft formation, while Angpt4 deficiency has no such effect.
source: In addition, in OIR model, Angpt1 (Lee et al., 2013) and Angpt2 (Hackett et al., 2002) deletions reduce neovascular tuft formation, while Angpt4 deficiency has no such effect (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by OIR model data showing no difference in avascular area between control and Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-E) and comparison with published data on Angpt1 and Angpt2 deletions.

claim: Angpt4 and ANGPT4 induce TIE2 phosphorylation in inter-endothelial junctions similarly to ANGPT1 but opposite to ANGPT2.
source: Similarly to ANGPT1, but opposite to ANGPT2, Angpt4 and ANGPT4 induced TIE2 phosphorylation in inter-endothelial junctions (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing pTIE2 staining at cell-cell junctions in Angpt4 and ANGPT4 stimulated cells (Figure 9A-B).

claim: In contrast to ANGPT1 and ANGPT2, Angpt4 and ANGPT4 do not bind to endothelial cell extracellular matrix.
source: In contrast to ANGPT1 and ANGPT2, Angpt4 and ANGPT4 did not bind to EC ECM (Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data showing minimal binding of Angpt4 and ANGPT4 to acellularized HUVEC ECM compared to ANGPT1 and ANGPT2 (Figure 9D).

claim: ANGPT4 does not induce TIE2 translocation to ECM contacts to a significant extent.
source: Interestingly, ANGPT2/TIE2 was mainly located in the cell rear and not incorporated into permanent EC-ECM contacts, while ANGPT4 did not induce TIE2 translocation to ECM contacts to a significant extent (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging of TIE2-GFP cells showing minimal ECM-bound TIE2 after ANGPT4 stimulation (Figure 9C).

claim: Substrate-bound Angpt4 and ANGPT4 fail to promote endothelial cell spreading.
source: When substrate-bound by solid phase antibody, Angpt4 and ANGPT4 failed to promote EC spreading that was induced by substrate-bound ANGPT1 (Figure 9E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell spreading assay data showing no increase in cell area on Angpt4 or ANGPT4 coated surfaces compared to control (Figure 9E-F).

claim: Angpt4 and ANGPT4 show lower affinity to TIE2 than ANGPT1 and ANGPT2 in ELISA and surface plasmon resonance assays.
source: In both assays, Angpt4 and ANGPT4 showed lower affinity to TIE2 than ANGPT1 and ANGPT2.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data (Figure 9G) and SPR data (Figure 9H) showing reduced binding of Angpt4 and ANGPT4 to TIE2 compared to ANGPT1 and ANGPT2.

claim: Among the angiopoietins, recovery rate in FRAP experiments is highest in Angpt4- and ANGPT4-stimulated cells, whereas ANGPT1 stimulation results in slowest recovery.
source: Among the ligands, recovery rate was highest in Angpt4- and ANGPT4-stimulated cells, whereas ANGPT1 stimulation resulted in slowest recovery.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data showing higher mobile fraction for Angpt4 and ANGPT4 compared to ANGPT1 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-C).

claim: ANGPT4 induces TIE2 tyrosine phosphorylation in HUVECs.
source: As previously published (Lee et al., 2004; Valenzuela et al., 1999), ANGPT4 induced TIE2 tyrosine phosphorylation in HUVECs.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data showing increased pTIE2 after ANGPT4 stimulation (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A-B) and is consistent with published reports.

claim: Angpt4 is less oligomerized than ANGPT4 and induces relatively low TIE2 activation in human endothelial cells when total TIE2 proteins are analyzed in western blot.
source: In comparison, Angpt4 was less oligomerized (Figure 9—figure supplement 2C–D) and induced relatively low TIE2 activation in human ECs when total TIE2 proteins were analyzed in western blot (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data showing lower pTIE2/TIE2 ratio for Angpt4 compared to ANGPT4 (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A-B) and SDS-PAGE showing less oligomerization (Figure 9—figure supplement 2C-D).

claim: Angpt4 expression is found in arterial smooth muscle cells in mouse mesenteric vessels.
source: To explore Angpt4 expression outside of the vasculature of the central nervous system, we analyzed mesenteric whole-mounts, where vasculature is readily visible for microscopic analysis. Interestingly, Angpt4 expression was found in arterial SMCs (Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by X-gal staining in Angpt4LacZ mice showing staining in mesenteric arteries (Figure 10B-C) and TEM showing staining in arterial SMCs (Figure 10D), confirmed by fate mapping (Figure 10G).

claim: Angpt4 is not expressed in primary astrocyte cultures from wild-type mouse brains.
source: However, in primary astrocyte cultures from WT mice (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A) or in Angpt4Cre; Rosa26mTmG brains (data not shown) we found no Angpt4 expression in astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data showing no Angpt4 mRNA in cultured brain astrocytes (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).

claim: ELISA does not detect Angpt4 in mouse serum.
source: ELISA did not detect Angpt4 in mouse serum and quantity of soluble Angpt4 was low in the eye preparations indicating that there is no significant amount of circulating Angpt4 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data showing no detectable Angpt4 in serum samples from P12 mice (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).

claim: The quantity of soluble Angpt4 is low in mouse eye preparations.
source: ELISA did not detect Angpt4 in mouse serum and quantity of soluble Angpt4 was low in the eye preparations indicating that there is no significant amount of circulating Angpt4 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data showing low levels of Angpt4 in retinal preparations from P12 mice (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Angpt4 is necessary for venous remodeling in the mouse retina.
source: In this study, we show that Angpt4 is necessary for venous remodeling and SMC maturation in the mouse retina.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including reduced vein diameter, defective SMC maturation, and impaired venous function in Angpt4-/- mice (Figures 4-7).

claim: Angpt4 is necessary for smooth muscle cell maturation in the mouse retina.
source: In this study, we show that Angpt4 is necessary for venous remodeling and SMC maturation in the mouse retina.
evidence: The claim is supported by ultrastructural data showing lack of myofilaments and fibrillar collagen in Angpt4-/- venous SMCs (Figure 5) and reduced SM22 expression (Figure 5G-J).

claim: Vascular smooth muscle cells are heterogenic cells that arise from multiple different origins in development.
source: Vascular SMCs are heterogenic cells that arise from multiple different origins in development (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from published literature.

claim: In the retina, vein smooth muscle cells can develop from neural crest origin.
source: In the retina, vein SMCs can develop from neural crest origin (Hughes and Chan-Ling, 2004; Trost et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is based on published literature.

claim: Mouse retinal vasculature develops postnatally in a highly organized and reproducible pattern.
source: Mouse retinal vasculature develops postnatally in a highly organized and reproducible pattern.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mouse retinal vascular development.

claim: Formation of astrocyte network in the superficial retinal layer occurs between embryonic day 19 and first postnatal day, preceding vascular development.
source: Formation of astrocyte network in the superficial retinal layer occurs between embryonic day 19 and first postnatal day thus preceding vascular development.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about retinal development.

claim: Astrocytes have a special function to form a template for sprouting endothelial cells.
source: Astrocytes have a special function to form a template for sprouting ECs, and together with retinal ganglion cells astrocytes express growth factors for angiogenic guidance and EC survival (Selvam et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on published literature.

claim: Astrocytes are a heterogeneous cell population.
source: Interestingly, astrocytes are known to be a heterogeneous cell population (Bayraktar et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is based on published literature.

claim: Angpt4+ astrocytes represent a specific subpopulation among glial cells.
source: Interestingly, astrocytes are known to be a heterogeneous cell population (Bayraktar et al., 2015) and our data indicates that Angpt4+ astrocytes represent a specific subpopulation among the glial cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the spatially restricted expression pattern of Angpt4 in peripheral retinal astrocytes (Figures 1-2) and lack of expression in brain astrocytes (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Angpt4 is especially important in the far peripheral segment of the retina that may develop via different pathway than central neural retina.
source: Intriguingly, genetic deletion revealed that Angpt4 is especially important in the far peripheral segment that may develop via different pathway than central neural retina (Venters et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on the peripheral-specific phenotype in Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 4) and published literature suggesting different developmental pathways.

claim: Clinical wide-field fundus imaging has identified a number of vascular diseases in humans in the peripheral retina that can affect the macula even though the primary defect is peripheral.
source: In addition, clinical wide-field fundus imaging has identified a number of vascular diseases in humans in the peripheral retina that can affect also macula even though primary defect is peripheral (Bajwa et al., 2015; Wessel et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on published clinical literature.

claim: Both Angpt1 and Angpt4 can be expressed in certain vascular smooth muscle cells.
source: The data is currently limited but suggests that both Angpt1 and Angpt4 can be expressed in certain vascular SMCs, raising interesting questions regarding ligand-specific and possible synergistic or additional effects of these Tie2 ligands.
evidence: The claim is based on the finding of Angpt4 expression in arterial SMCs (Figure 10) and published data on Angpt1-GFP expression in perivascular mural cells.

claim: Binding affinity of purified recombinant ANGPT4 protein to TIE2-Fc is considerably low when compared to ANGPT1.
source: Binding affinity of purified recombinant ANGPT4 protein to TIE2-Fc was considerably low when compared to ANGPT1 that binds TIE2 with high affinity.
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA and SPR data showing lower binding of ANGPT4 to TIE2 compared to ANGPT1 (Figure 9G-H).

claim: ANGPT4 binding to TIE2 is sufficient for TIE2 phosphorylation (activation) in cell culture assays.
source: Nevertheless, ANGPT4 to TIE2 binding was sufficient for TIE2 phosphorylation (activation) in cell culture assays.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data showing TIE2 phosphorylation after ANGPT4 stimulation (Figure 9A-B, Figure 9—figure supplement 2A-B).

claim: In mice, excess of both Angpt4 and ANGPT4 similarly induced angiogenic remodeling in corneal micropocket assay and in the trachea.
source: However, in mice, excess of both Angpt4 and ANGPT4 similarly induced angiogenic remodeling in corneal micropocket assay (Lee et al., 2004) and in the trachea (Kim et al., 2007), indicating that Angpt4 and ANGPT4 have similar in vivo functions.
evidence: The claim is based on published literature.

claim: Despite relatively low average sequence homology (65% identity) between Angpt4 and ANGPT4, certain functional characteristics are conserved.
source: Collectively, this suggests that despite relatively low average sequence homology (65% identity) between Angpt4 and ANGPT4, certain functional characteristics are still conserved.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that both Angpt4 and ANGPT4 induce similar responses in lumen formation assays and TIE2 activation (Figure 8, Figure 9).

claim: The spatiotemporally regulated expression of Angpt4 in astrocytes in the peripheral retina close to developing veins significantly differs from other angiopoietins.
source: Interestingly, observed spatiotemporally regulated expression of Angpt4 in astrocytes in the peripheral retina close to the developing veins significantly differed from other angiopoietins (Gale et al., 2002; Hackett et al., 2000; Hackett et al., 2002; Park et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of Angpt4 expression pattern (Figures 1-3) with published expression patterns of Angpt1 and Angpt2.

claim: The venous-specific phenotype in Angpt4-/- mice differs from defects in Angpt1-/- and Angpt2-/- retinas.
source: In addition, the venous-specific phenotype we characterize in Angpt4-/- mice also differs from defects in Angpt1-/- and Angpt2-/- retinas; Angpt1 deletion at P2–4 (analyzed at P5) caused reduced vascular density (Lee et al., 2013), and Angpt2 deficiency decreased sprouting of the primary plexus and delayed regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature at P10 (Gale et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of the venous-specific phenotype in Angpt4-/- mice (Figure 4) with published phenotypes of Angpt1-/- and Angpt2-/- mice.

claim: Angpt4 is functionally different from Angpt1 and Angpt2 based on its lack of effect on microvascular proliferation in the OIR model.
source: Although Angpt4 expression was induced in OIR model for ischemic retinopathy, Angpt4 deficiency did not affect microvascular proliferation, as has been found in Angpt1-/- (Lee et al., 2013) and Angpt2-/- mice (Hackett et al., 2002), suggesting that Angpt4 is functionally different.
evidence: The claim is based on OIR data showing no effect of Angpt4 deficiency on neovascularization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) compared to published effects of Angpt1 and Angpt2 deletions.

claim: In vitro characterization reveals redundant functions between angiopoietins 1 and 4.
source: On the other hand, in addition to ligand-specific effects, our in vitro characterization also revealed redundant functions between angiopoietins 1 and 4
evidence: The claim is based on in vitro data showing similar effects of ANGPT1 and ANGPT4 on lumen formation (Figure 8) and TIE2 activation in cell-cell junctions (Figure 9A-B).

claim: Differential, spatiotemporally regulated expression provides an important mechanism for complementary and sequential roles of angiopoietins to establish retinal circulation system.
source: suggesting that differential, spatiotemporally regulated expression provides an important mechanism for complementary and sequential roles of angiopoietins to establish retinal circulation system.
evidence: The claim is based on the distinct expression patterns of Angpt4 (Figures 1-3) compared to Angpt1 and Angpt2, and their different but complementary functions.

claim: TIE2 signaling appears particularly important to venous development based on reported venous-specific effects of inducible Tie2 deletion in retina and over-activating TIE2 mutations in venous malformations.
source: Moreover, based on reported venous-specific effects of inducible Tie2 deletion in retina (Chu et al., 2016) and over-activating TIE2 mutations in venous malformations (Kangas et al., 2018), Tie2 signaling appears particularly important to venous development that may contribute to the vessel-type-specific phenotype in Angpt4-/- mice.
evidence: The claim is based on published literature showing venous-specific effects of TIE2 signaling.

claim: Functional tests using fluorescent tracers show decreased venous flow in Angpt4-/- retinas.
source: In line with this suggestion, functional tests using fluorescent tracers showed decreased venous flow in Angpt4-/- retinas
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescein angiography and fluorosphere retention data (Figure 7).

claim: Alterations in neural cells in Angpt4-/- mice are secondary to venous remodeling defect.
source: and we propose that alterations in neural cells are secondary to venous remodeling defect.
evidence: The claim is based on the temporal sequence showing venous defects at P12 (Figure 4) preceding neuronal changes that are absent at P13 but present in adults (Figure 6C-D).

claim: Ultrastructural changes in neural cell somas in Angpt4-/- mice closely resemble intracellular edema.
source: While ultrastructural changes in neural cell somas closely resembled intracellular edema (Łotowska et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is based on TEM data showing enlarged, organelle-free cytoplasm (Figure 6D) and comparison with published descriptions of edema.

claim: In Angpt4-/- retinas, there are no changes in AQP4 or Kir4.1 expression.
source: In Angpt4-/- retinas, we found no changes in either AQP4 or Kir4.1, suggesting that water balance in Müller cells may be retained.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data showing no significant difference in AQP4 or Kir4.1 mRNA levels between WT and Angpt4-/- mice.

claim: Other neuronal cells in the inner nuclear layer may lack efficient water transport mechanism and be more vulnerable for alterations in fluid homeostasis due to diminished venous drainage.
source: Other neuronal cells in the INL (including amacrine and bipolar cells) may lack efficient water transport mechanism and thus be more vulnerable for alterations in fluid homeostasis due to diminished venous drainage that can be aggravated by the alterations in Müller cell architecture.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed cell swelling in INL neurons (Figure 6D) and known differences in water transport capabilities between cell types.

claim: There is no similar pathology in the literature to what is observed in Angpt4-/- mice (congenital decrease in vein diameter, venous SMC abnormality, diminished vein flow, but no inflammation or leakage).
source: In literature, there is no similar pathology than what we observe in Angpt4-/- mice (congenital decrease in vein diameter, venous SMC abnormality, diminished vein flow, but no inflammation or leakage), making direct comparison to the better characterized retinal pathologies (such as diabetic retinopathy and retinal vein occlusion) difficult.
evidence: The claim is based on the unique combination of phenotypes observed in Angpt4-/- mice and lack of similar reports in published literature.

claim: Interstitial edema may be prominent in retinal vascular diseases in which vascular barrier is disrupted, causing large increase in fluid entry that is excessive for exit mechanisms.
source: It may be possible that interstitial edema is prominent in retinal vascular diseases in which vascular barrier is disrupted, which causes large increase in fluid entry that is excessive for exit mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about mechanisms of edema formation in different disease contexts.

claim: The Angpt/Tie signaling pathway has emerged as an important target for drug development in ophthalmological diseases.
source: Angpt/Tie signaling pathway has emerged as an important target for drug development in ophthalmological diseases (Saharinen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on published literature.

claim: Thorough investigation of all angiopoietin ligands is necessary to fully evaluate the therapeutic potency of the Angpt/Tie signaling system.
source: In addition to providing novel insights into developmental angiogenesis, thorough investigation of all angiopoietin ligands is necessary to fully evaluate the therapeutic potency of this signaling system.
evidence: The claim is based on the finding that Angpt4 has distinct functions from other angiopoietins, suggesting the importance of understanding all family members.
